question: What purposes of the book are listed in verses 1 to 6, and to whom are they addressed?
Wisdom appears as a woman who cries out in the streets and squares: why present her in public places, and not in a temple or a school?
The word יִרְאָה (yir’ah, “fear”) appears in verse 7 and verse 29: what does it mean to call the fear of the LORD “the beginning of knowledge”?
The father warns against the sinners' invitation “come along with us”: what invitations from the group around you do you need to weigh more carefully?
What verbs of seeking does the father use in verses 1 to 4, and what does he promise to those who seek wisdom this way?
If wisdom must be sought with effort (v. 4), how should we understand that it is “the LORD [who] gives wisdom” (v. 6)?
The word אֹרַח (orach, “path, way”) appears in verses 8, 13, 19 and 20: what different paths does the chapter contrast?
The text compares the search for wisdom to that of someone seeking silver and hidden treasure: what have you been seeking with this same eagerness?
What does the father ask of his son regarding possessions and the LORD's discipline in verses 9 to 12?
What does it mean not to lean “on your own understanding” in a book that values understanding so highly?
The word חֵן (chen, “grace, favor”) appears in verses 4, 22 and 34: to whom is grace promised in each verse?
The text says not to tell your neighbor to come back tomorrow if you can help today: what help have you been putting off?
How does the father tell his own story of learning from his father in verses 3 and 4?
What images of light and darkness describe the two paths, and what do they suggest about how each develops over time?
The verb קָנָה (qanah, “acquire, buy”) is repeated in verses 5 and 7: what does this language of buying say about the value and the cost of wisdom?
“Guard your heart diligently, for from it flow the springs of life”: what has been entering your heart that needs more watchfulness?
How does the father describe the words of the adulteress and the end to which they lead?
What images of water, spring and fountain does the father use to speak of love in marriage, and what do they suggest about faithfulness?
The verb זוּר (zur, “be strange, foreign”) appears in verses 3, 10, 17 and 20: what makes someone or something “strange” in this chapter?
The text imagines someone lamenting at the end: “how I hated discipline”: what advice do you despise today that you may regret tomorrow?
What does the ant do, according to verses 6 to 8, and how is the sluggard described in contrast?
Why does the list of things the LORD hates begin with haughty eyes and end with one who “stirs up discord among brothers”?
The word עָצֵל (‘atsel, “sluggard”) appears in verses 6 and 9: what portrait of the sluggard does the chapter build in a few lines?
The father tells his son to free himself urgently from a rash pledge: what commitment made without thinking do you need to settle?
What does the father say he saw from the window, at what time of day and with what characters?
The woman speaks of sacrifices and vows fulfilled before making her invitation: what does this mixture of religion and seduction reveal?
The word מוֹדַע (moda‘, “kinsman”) appears in verse 4: what kind of relationship with wisdom and insight does the father propose to his son?
The young man “strolled down the road toward her house”: what paths do you usually take that bring you too close to what you want to avoid?
What qualities and gifts does Wisdom attribute to herself in verses 12 to 21?
Wisdom says she was with the LORD before creation; Jewish tradition associated her with the Torah and many Christians read her in light of Christ: what does the text itself say about her?
The word צֶדֶק (tsedeq, “righteousness”) appears in verses 8, 15 and 16: in what areas of life does Wisdom say righteousness should show itself?
Wisdom says “those who earnestly seek me will find me”: what would it be like to seek wisdom earnestly at this stage of your life?
What does Wisdom prepare, and whom does she invite, in verses 1 to 6?
The woman Folly uses almost the same words as Wisdom (vv. 4 and 16): what does this similarity teach about discerning invitations?
The verb לוּץ (lits, “mock”) appears in verses 7, 8 and 12: why is correcting a mocker so different from correcting a wise man?
The text says the wise man loves the one who rebukes him: how do you react when someone points out a mistake of yours?
Here begins the collection of “proverbs of Solomon”: how many times, in verses 11 to 21, do the sayings speak of mouth, lips or tongue, and what do they say about them?
What does it mean to say that “love covers all transgressions,” and how does this differ from hiding wrongdoing?
The word צַדִּיק (tsaddiq, “righteous”) appears in almost every verse of the chapter, nearly always next to the wicked: what does this constant contrast want to form in the reader?
“When words are many, sin is unavoidable”: in what conversations would you need to speak less?
What contrast do verses 24 to 26 draw between the one who gives freely and the one who withholds?
Why does a book of wisdom call dishonest scales “an abomination to the LORD,” placing commerce in the realm of faith?
The word תּוֹעֵבַה (to‘evah, “abomination”) appears in verses 1 and 20: what does the LORD detest, and what delights Him, in each verse?
The saying contrasts the one who “reveals secrets” with the one who “keeps a confidence”: what do you do with the secrets people entrust to you?
How do verses 15 to 23 describe the fool and the prudent man facing advice, insults and knowledge?
Why does a saying about caring for animals appear as a sign of who is righteous?
The word שֶׁקֶר (sheqer, “lie, falsehood”) appears in verses 17, 19 and 22: what does the chapter say about the duration and consequences of lying?
The text says some words pierce like a sword and that “a kind word” cheers the anxious heart: to whom could you speak a kind word today?
What do verses 7, 8 and 11 say about apparent wealth, real wealth and the way it is gained?
This saying about the “rod” has been used to justify violence against children: how can we read it honestly in its context and in light of the care the verse itself mentions?
The word נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “soul, life, appetite”) appears in verses 2, 4, 8 and 19: what meanings does it seem to have in each of these sayings?
“He who walks with the wise will become wise”: who are the people you spend the most time with, and what have they been forming in you?
What do verses 29 to 31 say about anger, envy and the way to treat the poor?
“There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death”: why can the appearance of being right be so deceptive?
The word אִוֶּלֶת (ivvelet, “folly”) appears six times in the chapter: what concrete behaviors does the chapter associate with this folly?
“The heart knows its own bitterness”: what pain or joy of yours do you feel no one else can fully share?
What do the two “better is... than...” sayings of verses 16 and 17 compare?
The text says the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable and the prayer of the upright pleases the LORD: what does this suggest about the relationship between worship and life?
The word תּוֹכֵחָה (tokhechah, “reproof”) appears in verses 5, 10, 31 and 32: what different reactions to reproof does the chapter describe?
“A gentle answer turns away wrath”: in what tense conversation of recent days would a gentler answer have changed the course?
What sayings about the king appear in verses 10 to 15, and what do they say about justice and favor?
The chapter opens and closes (vv. 1, 9 and 33) with the contrast between human plans and the LORD's action: how do these sayings balance human responsibility and divine sovereignty?
The word צְדָקָה (tsedaqah, “righteousness”) appears in verses 8, 12 and 31: in what spheres (personal life, politics, old age) does it appear?
“He who controls his temper is better than one who captures a city”: in what area do you most need self-control?
Which sayings of verses 1 to 6 speak of family life, and what values do they highlight?
Why compare the LORD's testing of hearts to the crucible for silver and the furnace for gold?
The verb אָהַב (ahav, “love”) appears in verse 17 and verse 19: what distinguishes the love of the friend, who loves “at all times,” from the love of one who “loves strife”?
“Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but whoever repeats a matter separates close friends”: what old matter do you keep bringing up?
Which sayings of verses 13, 15 and 17 deal with listening before concluding?
The saying speaks of friends who may bring ruin and of “a friend who stays closer than a brother”: what distinguishes one kind of friendship from the other?
The verb שָׂגַב (sagav, “be set on high, be safe”) appears in verse 10 and verse 11: what two sources of security do these neighboring sayings compare?
“Life and death are in the power of the tongue”: what words of yours have brought life or death to someone recently?
What do verses 4, 6 and 7 observe about the relationship between wealth, poverty and friendship?
“Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail”: does this discourage or free those who make plans?
The word דַּל (dal, “poor, weak”) appears in verse 4 and verse 17: how does verse 17 change the way of seeing the abandoned poor man of verse 4?
The saying says a man's glory “is to overlook an offense”: what offense could you let pass without holding on to it?
What do verses 10, 14 and 23 say about weights, measures and bargaining?
The question “who can say, ‘I have kept my heart pure’?” goes unanswered: what does it reveal about the human condition?
The word עֵצָה (‘etsah, “counsel, purpose”) appears in verses 5 and 18: where is counsel hidden, and how should it be used, according to these sayings?
“Do not say, ‘I will avenge this evil’; wait on the LORD”: is there a situation in which you are tempted to take justice into your own hands?
What relationship do the first three sayings establish between the human heart, the king and the LORD?
“A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD”: how does this saying unite human preparation and trust in God?
The word זֶבַח (zevach, “sacrifice”) appears in verses 3 and 27: what do these sayings say about the value of a sacrifice separated from righteousness?
“Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor” will not be answered either: what cry have you preferred not to hear?
From verse 17 a section of “sayings of the wise” begins: what goal does the teacher declare for it in verses 17 to 21?
“The rich and the poor have this in common: the LORD is Maker of them all”: what consequences does this common origin have for life together?
The word דַּל (dal, “poor”) appears in verses 9, 16 and 22: what attitudes toward the poor does the chapter praise and which does it condemn?
“Train up a child in the way he should go”: what habits or values did you receive early that still go with you, and which would you like to pass on?
What questions does the teacher ask in verse 29, and how do the following verses describe the one who lingers over wine?
Why is wealth compared to something that “will sprout wings and fly into the sky like an eagle”?
The word מוּסָר (musar, “discipline, instruction”) appears in verses 12, 13 and 23: how does discipline appear sometimes as something received and sometimes as something bought?
The text asks that the heart not envy sinners: at what moments do you feel envy of those who seem to prosper by doing wrong?
What did the wise man see as he passed by the sluggard's field, and what lesson did he draw from it?
The text does not accept the excuse “we did not know” regarding those being led away to death: what responsibility do these verses place on those who see injustice?
The verb קָנָא (qana’, “envy”) appears in verses 1 and 19: why do the wise come back twice to this warning?
“Do not gloat when your enemy falls”: how do you usually react when someone who hurt you goes through hardship?
According to verse 1, who copied these proverbs of Solomon, and what does this indicate about the formation of the book?
What might it mean to heap “burning coals on his head” by giving bread and water to someone who hates us?
The word כָּבוֹד (kavod, “glory, honor”) appears in verses 2 and 27: what glory befits God, kings, and those who seek glory for themselves?
“A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver”: what word are you waiting for the right moment to say?
What portrait of the sluggard do verses 13 to 16 paint, and with what comparisons?
Verses 4 and 5 seem to contradict each other about answering a fool: what does this pair of sayings teach about applying wisdom to situations?
The word כְּסִיל (kesil, “fool”) appears in almost all of verses 1 to 12: what characteristics of the fool does this sequence highlight?
“Without wood a fire goes out, and without a gossip a conflict ceases”: in what conversations could you stop being the wood?
What do verses 5, 6, 9 and 10 say about friendship, rebuke and closeness?
“As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another”: what kind of friendship does this saying describe, and what friction does it presuppose?
The verb גָּלָה (galah, “uncover, reveal”) lies behind the “open rebuke” of verse 5: why would something revealed be better than hidden love?
“Do not boast about tomorrow”: which of your plans have forgotten that tomorrow is not guaranteed?
What contrasts between the righteous and the wicked appear in verses 1 and 12, and how do the other sayings of the passage illustrate them?
“He who conceals his sins does not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy”: why do confessing and renouncing appear together?
The word תּוֹרָה (torah, “law, instruction”) appears in verses 4, 7 and 9: what place does the Torah have in this chapter of wisdom?
“Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but whoever hides his eyes will receive many curses”: from what needs around you have you turned your eyes?
What do verses 2, 4, 12, 14 and 16 say about the effect of righteous or wicked rulers on the people?
“Where there is no prophetic vision, the people cast off restraint”: what relationship does the verse draw between the prophetic word and the law that is kept?
The word תּוֹכֵחָה (tokhechah, “rebuke”) appears in verses 1 and 15: what happens to those who receive rebuke early and to those who resist it to the end?
“The fear of man is a snare”: in what decisions has fear of others' opinion weighed more than your trust in God?
How does Agur present himself in verses 1 to 3, and what questions does he ask in verse 4?
Agur asks for “neither poverty nor riches”: what spiritual dangers does he see in each extreme?
The verb שָׂבַע (sava‘, “be satisfied, be full”) appears in verses 9, 15, 16 and 22: what is never satisfied, and what danger is there in being too full?
Ants, rock badgers, locusts and lizards are small but wise: what small virtue of these creatures would you like to learn?
Who teaches King Lemuel in verses 1 to 9, and what advice does she give about wine and justice?
The poem of the wife of noble character, an acrostic in Hebrew, closes the book that began with Wisdom as a woman: what link might there be between the two figures?
The word חַיִל (chayil, “valor, strength, noble character”) describes the woman in verses 10 and 29 and is also used for warriors: what does this choice of word suggest about her portrait?
“Open your mouth for those with no voice”: for whom, who has no voice, could you speak?
